title: Given an unsorted array of `n` integers in the range `1` to `n` where some numbers may appear more than once and some numbers are therefore missing, return a list of all the numbers in `1..n` that do not appear. Solve in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (the output list does not count).
shortTitle: Find all Missing Numbers (Numbers Missing from 1..n)
keyPoints: Cyclic Sort places value v at index v-1, using the duplicate-safe guard nums[i] != nums[nums[i]-1].
After placement, every index where nums[i] != i+1 corresponds to a missing number.
Duplicate values naturally end up at leftover slots because their home index is already occupied.
The algorithm runs in O(n) time (each element swapped at most once) and O(1) extra space beyond the output list.
The negative-marking trick is an alternative: flip sign at index abs(v)-1 to mark presence.
The same Cyclic Sort loop also answers the find-all-duplicates question on the same input.

s1_definition.oneliner: Place v at index v-1; every slot where value != index+1 is a missing number.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Cyclic Sort with duplicates** – extends the basic Cyclic Sort pattern to arrays where some values appear more than once by using a duplicate-safe swap guard.
- **Placement rule** – value `v` belongs at index `v - 1`; the swap guard `nums[i] != nums[nums[i] - 1]` prevents infinite loops on duplicates.
- **Detection** – after placement, every index where `nums[i] != i + 1` marks a missing number from the range 1 to n.
- **Dual use** – the same placement loop also reveals duplicates: any value that could not be placed because its home was already occupied is a duplicate.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) extra space beyond the output list.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India expects one signed KYC form per customer numbered 1 to n, but some customers submitted duplicates and others never submitted. The clerk files each form in its matching locker. Any locker still holding the wrong form marks a form number that nobody ever submitted.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding all the missing numbers from an array over the range 1 to n, where duplicates are allowed, is the duplicate-tolerant extension of Cyclic Sort. I place each value at the index equal to the value minus one, but the critical change from the basic pattern is the swap guard: I compare the values at the two positions rather than the indices, so when a duplicate tries to swap into a slot that already holds the same value, the pointer advances instead of looping forever.

After the single placement pass, every slot whose stored value does not equal its index plus one marks a number that never appeared. The algorithm runs in linear time and uses no extra space beyond the output list. I know the negative-marking trick solves the same problem, but I favor Cyclic Sort because it leaves the array in an interpretable state and the identical loop also answers the find-all-duplicates question.

Edge cases include all elements being the same (maximum missing numbers), no duplicates (empty result), and a single-element array. The common mistake is using the wrong swap guard, which causes infinite loops on duplicates.

At the National Bank of India, this powered a KYC reconciliation job. Every customer in a batch was assigned a form number, some submitted duplicates, and others never submitted. Compliance needed the complete list of never-submitted form numbers, and the batches were too large to allocate a second tracking array.

Remember one sentence: place v at index v-1 with a duplicate-safe guard, and every mismatched slot after placement reveals a missing number.
